u{}_{\mu\lambda}V^\lambda$, what is the job of the Christoffel term?
options: It is the curvature tensor and vanishes only in flat space, in whatever coordinates are used.
It compensates for the changing basis vectors; it can be nonzero even in flat space.
It is the gravitational force on the vector, so that $\nabla_\mu V^\nu=0$ describes free fall.
It makes the derivative symmetric in its indices, so that the partial derivatives commute.
s3-l014-covariant-derivative-parallel-tr.explanation: Derivatives of components mix 'the vector changes' with 'the basis changes'. $\Gamma$ removes the second part. Curvature is a separate thing, extracted from commutators of covariant derivatives (the Riemann tensor).

s3-l014-covariant-derivative-parallel-tr.prompt: A vector is parallel-transported around a closed loop on a sphere and returns to its starting point. What happens?
options: It returns unchanged, because parallel transport keeps a vector parallel to itself and so cannot change its direction.
It returns rotated by $360^\circ$ regardless of the loop, because the sphere is a closed surface.
It returns rotated, but the angle depends on the vector's starting direction rather than on the loop.
It returns rotated by (enclosed area)/$R^2$: holonomy measures curvature, and on a plane it would be unchanged.
s3-l014-covariant-derivative-parallel-tr.explanation: Parallel transport keeps the length and angles between vectors fixed, but the final direction depends on the path. On a sphere of radius $R$ the holonomy angle is $A/R^2$. Around a geodesic triangle with three $90^\circ$ angles (an octant), the vector rotates $90^\circ$.

s3-l014-covariant-derivative-parallel-tr.prompt: On a sphere, a loop runs from the north pole down a meridian (longitude $0^\circ$) to the equator, along the equator to longitude $60^\circ$, then back up that meridian to the pole. A vector is parallel-transported around the loop. By what angle, in degrees, does it rotate relative to its starting direction?
s3-l014-covariant-derivative-parallel-tr.explanation: The rotation angle in radians is (enclosed area)/$R^2$ $= \Delta\phi\,(1-\cos\theta_{\max}) = (\pi/3)(1 - 0) = 1.0472$, i.e. 60 degrees. (The loop's three corners have angles $90^\circ, 90^\circ, 60^\circ$, an angle excess of $60^\circ$.)

s3-l014-covariant-derivative-parallel-tr.prompt: Why are geodesics sometimes called the 'straightest possible' curves?
options: A geodesic parallel-transports its own tangent vector, never turning relative to the geometry.
They are always the shortest paths between two points, in any geometry whatsoever.
All the Christoffel symbols vanish along them, in every coordinate system.
Their coordinate acceleration $d^2x^\mu/d\lambda^2$ vanishes in all coordinate systems.
s3-l014-covariant-derivative-parallel-tr.explanation: In curved space, 'straight' means the tangent stays parallel to itself. Geodesics are only locally extremal (on a sphere the long way around is also a geodesic; in Lorentzian geometry timelike geodesics maximise proper time). The coordinate acceleration need not vanish.

s3-l014-covariant-derivative-parallel-tr.prompt: Explain why demanding that the covariant derivative preserve the metric ($\nabla g = 0$) and have no torsion fixes the Christoffel symbols uniquely, and what the metric-compatibility condition means physically.
s3-l014-covariant-derivative-parallel-tr.rubric:
Full credit: (1) metric compatibility means that lengths and angles are preserved under parallel transport (inner products of parallel-transported vectors stay constant); (2) torsion-free means $\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu
u}=\Gamma^\lambda_{
u\mu}$ (infinitesimal parallelograms close); (3) these two conditions determine $\Gamma$ completely from the metric via the Christoffel formula (permuting indices on $
abla g=0$ and combining).
s3-l014-covariant-derivative-parallel-tr.modelAnswer:
Metric compatibility says that when two vectors are parallel-transported, their lengths and the angle between them do not change, so transport is a pure rotation, which fits the idea that the geometry defines lengths. Torsion-free means $\Gamma^\lambda{}_{\mu
u}$ is symmetric in its lower indices. Writing out $
abla_\lambda g_{\mu
u}=0$ with its three index permutations and combining them gives $\Gamma$ in terms of derivatives of $g_{\mu
u}$ alone; no further freedom remains.

s3-l015-riemann-curvature-geodesic-devia.prompt: Two freely falling particles start at rest relative to each other, and later their separation begins to change. What does this tell you?
options: A force acts between the particles in addition to gravity, since free fall alone would keep them at rest relative to each other.
Their frames are non-inertial, and a change to a better inertial frame would remove the relative acceleration.
Spacetime is curved: the tidal term $-R^\mu{}_{\nu\rho\sigma}u^\nu\xi^\rho u^\sigma$ is nonzero in every coordinate system.
They have different masses and so fall at different rates, which violates the equivalence principle.
s3-l015-riemann-curvature-geodesic-devia.explanation: By the equivalence principle all free fall is universal, so mass differences are irrelevant. Relative acceleration between nearby geodesics is a physical, coordinate-independent measure of curvature (tidal forces), exactly what the Newtonian tidal tensor $\partial_i\partial_j\Phi$ represents.

s3-l015-riemann-curvature-geodesic-devia.prompt: The Newtonian tidal acceleration across a body of height $L$ at distance $r$ from a mass $M$ (Riemann in the weak-field limit) is $2GML/r^3$ along the radial direction. For a 1.8 m person standing on Earth's surface ($GM_\oplus = 3.986\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^3/s^2}$, $R = 6.371\times10^6$ m), find the head-to-foot difference in Earth's gravitational acceleration, in $\mu\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
s3-l015-riemann-curvature-geodesic-devia.explanation: $2GML/R^3 = 5.55\ \mu\mathrm{m/s^2}$, about $5\times10^{-7}\,g$: undetectable by the person, which is why free fall locally feels like zero gravity. The Moon's tidal field on the oceans is the same effect accumulated over a planet-size scale.

s3-l015-riemann-curvature-geodesic-devia.prompt:
The Riemann tensor is defined through $[
abla_\mu,
abla_
u]V^ho = R^ho{}_{\sigma\mu
u}V^\sigma$. What is the geometric meaning of this?
options: It is the failure of the metric to be diagonal in a given coordinate system.
It records the fact that partial derivatives do not commute in curved coordinates.
It measures how far the geodesics differ from straight lines in a chosen coordinate system.
Curvature is the failure of covariant derivatives to commute: path dependence of transport.
s3-l015-riemann-curvature-geodesic-devia.explanation: Partial derivatives always commute. The Riemann tensor arises when the Christoffel terms in $\nabla$ fail to cancel in the commutator. In flat space with Cartesian coordinates, $R=0$; the polar-coordinate Christoffel terms cancel exactly there.

s3-l015-riemann-curvature-geodesic-devia.prompt: A generic Riemann tensor in $n$ dimensions has $n^2(n^2-1)/12$ independent components after using its symmetries (this gives 20 for spacetime, $n=4$). How many does it have in $n = 3$ dimensions?
s3-l015-riemann-curvature-geodesic-devia.explanation: $n^2(n^2-1)/12 = 9\cdot8/12 = 6$. In $n=2$ the formula gives 1: the single Gaussian curvature $K = 1/R^2$ for a sphere. In 3D the Ricci tensor (also 6 components) carries all the curvature information; in 4D there are 10 more (Weyl) components that can exist in vacuum.

s3-l015-riemann-curvature-geodesic-devia.prompt: The Christoffel symbols can be made to vanish at a point by a choice of coordinates, but the Riemann tensor cannot. Explain what this says physically about gravity and the equivalence principle.
s3-l015-riemann-curvature-geodesic-devia.rubric: Full credit: (1) Christoffels are not tensors, they encode coordinate-dependent connection (inertial 'forces'), and can be set to zero at a point (local inertial frame); (2) Riemann is a tensor built from second derivatives of the metric, so it is the same in all frames: curvature; (3) physical meaning: gravity's local effects (acceleration) can be removed (equivalence principle) but tidal effects, differences over distance, cannot; so spacetime is curved.
s3-l015-riemann-curvature-geodesic-devia.modelAnswer: The Christoffel symbols describe the acceleration that arises from your choice of frame, which in free fall can be cancelled at a point: that is the equivalence principle. The Riemann tensor involves second derivatives of the metric and is a genuine tensor, so if it is nonzero in one frame it is nonzero in all frames. It describes tidal effects (relative accelerations of nearby free-falling particles) that no choice of free-falling frame can remove: that is the invariant content of gravity.

s3-l016-ricci-bianchi-einstein-tensor.prompt: The Ricci scalar of a 2-sphere of radius $R$ is $\mathcal R = 2/R^2$ (twice the Gaussian curvature). What is its value, in $\mathrm{m^{-2}}$, for a sphere of radius $R = 2$ m?
s3-l016-ricci-bianchi-einstein-tensor.explanation: $\mathcal R = 2/R^2 = 2/4 = 0.5\ \mathrm{m^{-2}}$. It is positive for a sphere, and zero for a plane (or a cylinder): the Ricci scalar is the intrinsic curvature, independent of embedding.

s3-l016-ricci-bianchi-einstein-tensor.prompt:
What is the physical consequence of the contracted Bianchi identity $
abla_\mu G^{\mu
u} = 0$ for the Einstein equation $G_{\mu
u} = (8\pi G/c^4)T_{\mu
u}$?
options: The total energy of the universe is exactly conserved, as in Newtonian mechanics.
The source must satisfy $\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0$: local energy-momentum conservation.
The curvature must vanish wherever there is no matter, so vacuum spacetime is flat.
The metric is fixed up to coordinate choice, leaving no freedom to specify initial conditions.
s3-l016-ricci-bianchi-einstein-tensor.explanation: The divergence of the left side vanishes identically (a geometric fact), so the right side must also be divergence-free. This is local conservation; a global conserved energy exists only when the spacetime has a timelike Killing vector (a time-translation symmetry).

s3-l016-ricci-bianchi-einstein-tensor.prompt: The vacuum Einstein equation is $R_{\mu\nu} = 0$. Does this imply flat spacetime?
options: Yes: with no Ricci curvature there is no source, so the Riemann tensor must vanish as well.
Yes: the Ricci tensor is a contraction of Riemann, and contractions preserve all of the information.
No. Schwarzschild has $R_{\mu\nu}=0$ outside the mass yet nonzero Weyl curvature (tides).
Yes, but only without a cosmological constant; with $\Lambda\neq0$ vacuum is curved.
s3-l016-ricci-bianchi-einstein-tensor.explanation: The Riemann tensor has 20 components in 4D; the Ricci tensor accounts for only 10 of them. The remaining 10 (the Weyl tensor) can be nonzero in vacuum and carry the tidal field of a distant source and gravitational waves.

s3-l016-ricci-bianchi-einstein-tensor.prompt:
Why is the Einstein tensor $G_{\mu
u} = R_{\mu
u} - 	frac12 R g_{\mu
u}$, rather than $R_{\mu
u}$ alone, the natural geometric counterpart of $T_{\mu
u}$?
options: It is symmetric, second order in derivatives of the metric, and divergence-free like $T_{\mu\nu}$.
The Einstein tensor contains the Weyl curvature, which is the part directly sourced by matter.
The Einstein tensor is identical to the Riemann tensor in four dimensions, so the choice is only notation.
It is the only curvature-built tensor that vanishes in flat space, so it is the only one that can couple to matter.
s3-l016-ricci-bianchi-einstein-tensor.explanation: Requirements: tensor, symmetric, linear in second derivatives, divergence-free. Together with the Newtonian limit they essentially fix $G_{\mu\nu}$ (up to the cosmological-constant term). Hilbert's action $\int R\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x$ gives the same equation.

s3-l016-ricci-bianchi-einstein-tensor.prompt: The Ricci and Weyl parts of the curvature play different physical roles. Explain in your own words what each one does to a small ball of freely falling test particles.
s3-l016-ricci-bianchi-einstein-tensor.rubric: Full credit: (1) Ricci curvature, sourced locally by matter, changes the volume of the ball (focusing/convergence of geodesics); (2) Weyl curvature, the part that can exist in vacuum, distorts the ball's shape (tidal stretch and squeeze) at constant volume, to first order, and carries gravitational waves; (3) both are parts of the geodesic deviation from the Riemann tensor.
s3-l016-ricci-bianchi-einstein-tensor.modelAnswer: The trace part of the geodesic-deviation tensor (the Ricci curvature) tells how the volume of a small ball of test particles changes: it is determined by the matter present locally, so matter focuses geodesics (like $\nabla^2\Phi = 4\pi G\rho$). The trace-free Weyl part leaves the volume unchanged to first order but stretches the ball in one direction and squeezes it in others; this tidal distortion remains in vacuum and is what a passing gravitational wave produces.

s3-l017-stress-energy-einstein-equation.prompt: In GR the acceleration of the cosmic expansion depends on $\rho + 3p/c^2$. Why does pressure act as a source of gravity?
options: Pressure (momentum flux $T^{ii}$) is part of $T^{\mu\nu}$, and the whole tensor is the source of gravity.
It does not: pressure enters only through the conversion $\rho\to\rho c^2$ and is a bookkeeping device.
Pressure pushes matter outward and so counteracts gravity, exactly as in the Newtonian hydrostatic equation.
Pressure raises the temperature, which increases the rest mass of the particles.
s3-l017-stress-energy-einstein-equation.explanation: In Newtonian gravity only $\rho$ sources $\Phi$. In GR the source is $T^{\mu\nu}$, and for a perfect fluid $T^{00} = \rho c^2$ and $T^{ii} = p$. Positive pressure increases gravitational attraction; dark energy's negative pressure ($p = -\rho c^2$) gives repulsion.

s3-l017-stress-energy-einstein-equation.prompt: How does the Newtonian limit $\nabla^2\Phi = 4\pi G\rho$ emerge from the Einstein equation, and what fixes the factor $8\pi G/c^4$?
options: The factor $8\pi$ follows from pure geometry, independent of experiment, and Newton's $G$ then enters via the metric.
All ten components contribute equally in the limit, and their sum reduces to $\nabla^2\Phi$.
For weak static fields and slow dust only the 00 component matters; matching Poisson fixes $8\pi G/c^4$.
It needs strong fields and relativistic speeds; in the Newtonian limit the equation reduces to $\nabla\Phi=0$.
s3-l017-stress-energy-einstein-equation.explanation: The proportionality of $G_{\mu\nu}$ and $T_{\mu\nu}$ is required by the Bianchi identity; the number $8\pi G/c^4$ is fixed by demanding that the Newtonian limit be Poisson's equation with the measured $G$.

s3-l017-stress-energy-einstein-equation.prompt: Dust has rest-frame mass density $\rho = 1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$. An observer moves relative to the dust at $v = 0.6c$. What energy density $T^{00}$ (in $\mathrm{J/m^3}$) does this observer measure, using $T^{\mu\nu} = \rho u^\mu u^\nu$ with $u^0 = \gamma c$?
s3-l017-stress-energy-einstein-equation.explanation: $T^{00} = \gamma^2\rho c^2$ with $\gamma = 1.250$, giving 1.404e+14 J/m³, a factor of $\gamma^2 = 1.562$ larger than the rest-frame $\rho c^2$ because one $\gamma$ comes from the energy per particle and one from length contraction of the volume.

s3-l017-stress-energy-einstein-equation.prompt: The Einstein equation implies $\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu} = 0$. Does this mean the total energy of the universe is conserved?
options: Yes: since the divergence of $T$ vanishes, the volume integral of $T^{00}$ is constant in any spacetime.
No: it is a local law; a conserved total energy needs a timelike Killing vector (a time-translation symmetry).
Yes, but only with a cosmological constant, which supplies the required symmetry.
No, because $\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0$ holds only in the Newtonian limit and fails when gravity is strong.
s3-l017-stress-energy-einstein-equation.explanation: In flat space $\partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0$ integrates to a conserved charge via Gauss's theorem. With a covariant divergence the Christoffel terms exchange energy with the gravitational field, and integrals of components are not coordinate-invariant. Noether's theorem needs a symmetry.

s3-l017-stress-energy-einstein-equation.prompt: Explain in your own words the statement 'matter tells spacetime how to curve; spacetime tells matter how to move', and identify which equation encodes each half.
s3-l017-stress-energy-einstein-equation.rubric:
Full credit: (1) Einstein field equation: $T_{\mu
u}$ (matter, energy and stress) determines the curvature $G_{\mu
u}$; (2) geodesic equation (or $
abla_\mu T^{\mu
u}=0$) tells matter to follow geodesics of the curved geometry; (3) points out the loop: the equations are nonlinear and coupled; possible mention that Newtonian limit reproduces Poisson and $\ddot{\mathbf x}=-
abla\Phi$.
s3-l017-stress-energy-einstein-equation.modelAnswer:
The Einstein equation $G_{\mu
u} = 8\pi G T_{\mu
u}/c^4$ says the energy, momentum, and stress of matter determine the curvature of spacetime. The geodesic equation (a consequence of $
abla_\mu T^{\mu
u}=0$) says free matter follows the straightest paths in that geometry. In the Newtonian limit these become Poisson's equation (matter sources the potential) and $\ddot{\mathbf x} = -
abla\Phi$ (the potential moves the matter).

s3-l018-spherical-symmetry-birkhoff.prompt: A spherical star pulsates radially in and out. Birkhoff's theorem says what about the gravitational field outside it?
options: The exterior metric oscillates at the pulsation frequency, which produces monopole gravitational waves.
The exterior is Schwarzschild only for a static star; a pulsating star has a time-dependent exterior.
The pulsation radiates quadrupole waves, since the star's mass distribution varies with time.
It is exactly Schwarzschild for the constant total mass, so the pulsation is invisible outside.
s3-l018-spherical-symmetry-birkhoff.explanation: Birkhoff's theorem: any spherically symmetric vacuum solution is Schwarzschild (hence static). It is the GR analogue of Newton's shell theorem and of the absence of monopole radiation in electromagnetism. Gravitational waves need a time-varying quadrupole moment, which a spherical pulsation lacks.

s3-l018-spherical-symmetry-birkhoff.prompt: Compared with the Newtonian hydrostatic equation $dp/dr = -G\rho m/r^2$, how do the extra relativistic factors in the TOV equation change the physics of dense stars?
options: The corrections weaken gravity in dense stars, so GR allows heavier stars than Newtonian theory does.
The corrections matter only for rotating stars, because TOV is the extension that includes frame dragging.
Pressure itself gravitates and the geometric factor grows, so every correction strengthens gravity, implying a maximum mass.
Pressure still only opposes gravity, as in the Newtonian equation; the factors change numbers, not the qualitative behaviour.
s3-l018-spherical-symmetry-birkhoff.explanation: Pressure holds a star up but also adds to the source of gravity; at high compactness the second effect wins and no pressure can stabilize the star. For neutron stars this gives the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff maximum mass of roughly $2$-$3\,M_\odot$.

s3-l018-spherical-symmetry-birkhoff.prompt: When solving the vacuum Einstein equations for a static spherically symmetric metric, why does the integration constant become $2GM/c^2$?
options: Matching $g_{00}\approx-(1-2GM/rc^2)$ at large $r$ identifies the one free constant with the mass.
It is the radius at which the pressure of the stellar interior falls to zero.
The field equations require the horizon to sit at $2GM/c^2$ for consistency.
It is arbitrary and can take any value, since the source's mass plays no role in the vacuum solution.
s3-l018-spherical-symmetry-birkhoff.explanation: The vacuum equations fix the functional form of the metric; the constant measures the source's strength, and its physical meaning is read off from the weak-field limit. The same solution works outside any spherical body, including a star, because of Birkhoff's theorem.

s3-l018-spherical-symmetry-birkhoff.prompt: The Buchdahl bound says any static, spherical star has $R > 9GM/(4c^2)$. What is the smallest possible radius, in km, of a $1.4\,M_\odot$ neutron star? ($GM_\odot/c^2 = 1.477$ km.)
s3-l018-spherical-symmetry-birkhoff.explanation: $R_{\min} = (9/4)(1.4)(1.477\ \mathrm{km}) = 4.65$ km, only 12.5% bigger than the Schwarzschild radius (4.13 km). Actual neutron stars have $R\approx 11$-$13$ km, a factor 2.5 or so above the bound.

s3-l018-spherical-symmetry-birkhoff.prompt: State the Buchdahl bound in words and explain what it implies for a star more compact than the bound.
s3-l018-spherical-symmetry-birkhoff.rubric: Full credit: (1) a static spherical star in GR (with non-increasing density) must have radius greater than $9/4$ times $GM/c^2$ ($9/8\, r_s$); (2) pressure gravitates, so squeezing further needs ever more pressure, which diverges at the bound; (3) hence no static configuration exists for more compact objects: the star must collapse, ending as a black hole.
s3-l018-spherical-symmetry-birkhoff.modelAnswer: A static, spherical star in general relativity cannot have a radius smaller than $9GM/4c^2$, i.e. $9/8$ of its Schwarzschild radius. Close to this limit the central pressure required for equilibrium diverges, because pressure adds to gravity. Therefore a body more compact than the bound cannot be held up by any matter; it must collapse to a black hole.

s3-l019-linearized-gravity-wave-emission.prompt: Why does gravity have no monopole or dipole radiation, so the leading gravitational radiation is quadrupolar?
options: Spherically symmetric sources do not exist in nature, so monopole radiation is impossible.
They exist but are too weak compared with the quadrupole for any known astrophysical source.
Gravitational waves are transverse, and a transverse wave cannot be produced by a dipole.
Conservation of energy and momentum forbids both monopole and dipole radiation.
s3-l019-linearized-gravity-wave-emission.explanation: In electromagnetism a dipole is allowed because charges come in both signs, and the dipole moment can change even if total charge is conserved. For mass, $\ddot{\mathbf d} \propto \dot{\mathbf P} = 0$ by momentum conservation. Thus the first allowed radiation is from the mass quadrupole: $h\sim G\ddot Q/(c^4 r)$.

s3-l019-linearized-gravity-wave-emission.prompt: The linearized field equation $\Box\bar h_{\mu\nu} = -16\pi G T_{\mu\nu}/c^4$ is solved with a retarded Green's function, just as for the retarded potentials of electrodynamics. What is the physical meaning of evaluating the source at $t - r/c$?
options: The field depends on the source at all times, past and future, averaged symmetrically.
The field at $(t,r)$ is set by the source at time $t-r/c$: changes propagate outward at $c$.
Gravity acts instantaneously, and $t-r/c$ is only the delay in the measuring apparatus.
It is the time a graviton is emitted, after which it travels at a speed set by its energy.
s3-l019-linearized-gravity-wave-emission.explanation: The retarded solution is selected by causality. The $1/r$ fall-off of the radiative part means energy flux $\propto 1/r^2$ so that a fixed amount of energy crosses every large sphere.

s3-l019-linearized-gravity-wave-emission.prompt: Which of these systems radiates gravitational waves in the quadrupole approximation?
options: A perfectly spherical star rotating uniformly about an axis through its centre at constant angular velocity.
A thin rod tumbling end over end: its quadrupole changes in time, radiating at twice the rotation frequency.
A spherical star pulsating radially, expanding and contracting while staying exactly spherical.
A perfectly axisymmetric disk spinning at constant angular velocity about its own symmetry axis.
s3-l019-linearized-gravity-wave-emission.explanation: The radiation requires $\dddot Q_{ij}\neq 0$. Rotation about a symmetry axis or radial pulsations leave the mass quadrupole constant or zero. The rod's quadrupole returns to itself after half a turn, hence frequency $2f_{\rm rot}$. A circular binary radiates the same way.

s3-l019-linearized-gravity-wave-emission.prompt: Two $1.4\,M_\odot$ neutron stars orbit each other on a circular orbit of separation $a = 1.95\times10^9$ m (similar to the Hulse-Taylor pulsar). Use the quadrupole formula's result $t_{\rm coal} = \dfrac{5}{256}\dfrac{c^5 a^4}{G^3 m_1 m_2 (m_1+m_2)}$ to estimate the time to merger, in years. ($G=6.674\times10^{-11}$, $M_\odot = 1.989\times10^{30}$ kg.)
s3-l019-linearized-gravity-wave-emission.explanation: $t_{\rm coal} = 5.33e+16$ s $\approx 1.69e+09$ yr, about 1.7 billion years for a circular orbit (the real PSR B1913+16 is eccentric, $e\approx0.62$, which speeds the merger up to about 300 Myr). Since $t\propto a^4$, halving the separation shortens the time by a factor of 16.

s3-l019-linearized-gravity-wave-emission.prompt:
Linearized gravity, with $g_{\mu
u} = \eta_{\mu
u} + h_{\mu
u}$, looks a lot like electromagnetism with retarded potentials. List one important similarity and one important difference between the two radiation problems.
s3-l019-linearized-gravity-wave-emission.rubric: Full credit: similarity: wave equation with source in Lorenz/harmonic gauge solved by retarded Green's function; waves at $c$; $1/r$ radiation field; or energy flux. Difference: gravity's source is a rank-2 tensor / spin-2 so quadrupole is leading (dipole forbidden by momentum conservation), whereas EM has dipole radiation from vector source; or gravity gravitates (nonlinear), or only one sign of charge.
s3-l019-linearized-gravity-wave-emission.modelAnswer: Both are wave equations for a potential ($A_\mu$ or $\bar h_{\mu\nu}$) sourced by a conserved current ($J_\mu$ or $T_{\mu\nu}$), in Lorenz gauge, solved by retarded solutions; the radiation travels at $c$ and falls off as $1/r$. The difference is that the gravitational source is a tensor with only one sign of charge, so conservation of momentum kills the dipole term and the lowest radiation is quadrupolar (spin 2), and that the full theory is nonlinear because gravity itself carries energy.

s3-l020-frw-friedmann-from-einstein.prompt: In the FRW picture, distant galaxies recede from us. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Galaxies were flung outward from a central point and move through a fixed background space at speeds set by the initial explosion.
Space expands inside every bound system, atoms and galaxies included, but our rulers expand too, so we cannot measure it.
Galaxies move through space, and those receding faster than $c$ have broken special relativity locally.
Comoving galaxies keep fixed coordinates while $a(t)$ grows: the space between them stretches.
s3-l020-frw-friedmann-from-einstein.explanation: The metric $ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + a(t)^2[\ldots]$ tells you proper distance between comoving points is $a(t)\chi$. Recession speed $v = H d$ can exceed $c$ at large distance without violating relativity, which only restricts local motion relative to the Hubble flow.

s3-l020-frw-friedmann-from-einstein.prompt: The acceleration equation is $\ddot a/a = -\tfrac{4\pi G}{3}(\rho + 3p/c^2) + \Lambda c^2/3$. What is needed for the expansion to accelerate?
options: A component with sufficiently negative pressure, $p<-\rho c^2/3$, such as a cosmological constant.
A very large positive pressure, which pushes the universe outward faster than gravity pulls it in.
A negative mass density, since any positive density always decelerates the expansion.
A matter density above the critical density, whose extra gravity speeds the expansion up.
s3-l020-frw-friedmann-from-einstein.explanation: Positive pressure adds to deceleration in GR because it contributes to the gravitating source. Negative pressure that is more negative than $-\rho c^2/3$ makes $\rho + 3p/c^2<0$ and yields repulsion. This is what dark energy is inferred to do.

s3-l020-frw-friedmann-from-einstein.prompt: In a flat universe dominated by matter, $a\propto t^{2/3}$ and the age is $t_0 = 2/(3H_0)$. For $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc (1 Mpc $= 3.086\times10^{22}$ m), find $t_0$ in billions of years.
s3-l020-frw-friedmann-from-einstein.explanation: $H_0 = 2.269e-18\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, so $t_0 = 2/(3H_0) = 9.31$ Gyr. This is shorter than the age of the oldest stars and the ΛCDM value ($\approx 13.8$ Gyr), one of the early arguments for a cosmological constant.

s3-l020-frw-friedmann-from-einstein.prompt: Why did radiation dominate the early universe, while matter dominates later and (today) dark energy takes over?
options: Radiation is gradually converted into matter as the universe cools, and matter into dark energy as structures form.
All three components dilute the same way with volume, so their ratios are fixed by the initial conditions.
Matter dilutes as $a^{-3}$, radiation as $a^{-4}$, and Lambda not at all, so the slowest-diluting wins late.
Radiation density falls as $a^{-2}$ because photons spread over areas, matter as $a^{-3}$, and Lambda as $a^{-4}$.
s3-l020-frw-friedmann-from-einstein.explanation: The Friedmann equation then gives $a\propto t^{1/2}$ for radiation, $t^{2/3}$ for matter, and $e^{Ht}$ for Lambda. The universe passes through these epochs in that order.

s3-l020-frw-friedmann-from-einstein.prompt: The Newtonian derivation of the Friedmann equation uses a shell of dust in a gravitating sphere. State two things that the GR derivation adds, and explain the physical meaning of the curvature constant $k$.
s3-l020-frw-friedmann-from-einstein.rubric: Full credit: (1) GR gives meaning to $k$: the spatial curvature of the universe (closed $k=+1$, flat $0$, open $-1$), whereas in Newton it is just an energy (integration) constant; (2) pressure is a source of gravity ($\rho+3p/c^2$), also Lambda and radiation fall naturally into the formalism; (3) it applies to the whole of space including radiation and beyond the horizon, consistent with relativity.
s3-l020-frw-friedmann-from-einstein.modelAnswer: In the Newtonian derivation the term $-kc^2/a^2$ is just the total energy of a test shell. In GR it is the curvature of space itself: $k=+1$ is a closed universe like a 3-sphere, $k=0$ is flat, and $k=-1$ is open (negatively curved), with flatness corresponding to the critical density. GR also tells us that pressure gravitates (the $\rho + 3p/c^2$ combination), which lets radiation and dark energy be included consistently.

s3-l021-horizons-observations-lcdm.prompt: The particle horizon today is about 46 billion light-years in comoving distance, though the universe is only 13.8 billion years old. How is this possible?
options: Light travelled faster than $c$ during the early universe, covering a larger distance than $ct$.
The age of the universe is underestimated; the true age must be about 46 billion years.
Distant galaxies move through space faster than $c$ relative to us, which carries them 46 Gly away.
Light has travelled since the Big Bang, but space expanded meanwhile, carrying its sources farther away.
s3-l021-horizons-observations-lcdm.explanation: The horizon is $d_{\rm hor} = a(t)\int c\,dt'/a(t')$, which exceeds $ct$ when $a$ grows. It marks the farthest point we could, in principle, have received signals from. It is not an edge of the universe.

s3-l021-horizons-observations-lcdm.prompt: What do the labels closed ($k=+1$), flat ($k=0$) and open ($k=-1$) FRW models tell us?
options: The universe's fate: closed ones always recollapse, open ones always expand, flat ones stall, whatever the cosmological constant.
The geometry of space at fixed cosmic time; with Lambda, geometry alone does not fix the fate of the expansion.
A closed universe has a boundary beyond which there is nothing, and an open universe is infinite but has an edge.
Flat means no matter content, while closed and open give the sign of the matter's net energy.
s3-l021-horizons-observations-lcdm.explanation: In matter-only models the spatial curvature is tied to the fate of the expansion. With $\Lambda$, a closed universe can expand forever. Observations (CMB) find $|\Omega_k|\lesssim 10^{-3}$, consistent with flat.

s3-l021-horizons-observations-lcdm.prompt: Distant Type Ia supernovae are fainter than a matter-only decelerating universe would predict. What is the most natural interpretation?
options: The universe is decelerating even more strongly than a matter-only model predicts.
Space is positively curved, which dims every distant source by an overall factor.
The expansion accelerated recently, which requires something like a cosmological constant.
Gravity is stronger at large distances, which slows the light coming from supernovae.
s3-l021-horizons-observations-lcdm.explanation: Luminosity distance depends on the integral $\int dz/H(z)$. A larger distance at given redshift means $H$ was lower in the past relative to a matter-only model, i.e. acceleration. Combined with the CMB (flat geometry) and BAO, this gives $\Omega_m\approx0.3$, $\Omega_\Lambda\approx0.7$.

s3-l021-horizons-observations-lcdm.prompt: In a flat $\Lambda$CDM universe with $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc, $\Omega_m = 0.3$ and $\Omega_\Lambda = 0.7$, $H(z) = H_0\sqrt{0.3(1+z)^3 + 0.7}$. Evaluate the comoving distance $\chi(z) = \int_0^z c\,dz'/H(z')$ to a galaxy at $z = 1$, in Mpc. ($c = 2.998\times10^5$ km/s.)
s3-l021-horizons-observations-lcdm.explanation: Numerical integration gives $\chi = 3304$ Mpc (about 10.8 billion light-years). The integrand falls as $H$ grows, so the distance is less than the naive $cz/H_0 = 4283$ Mpc.

s3-l021-horizons-observations-lcdm.prompt: Cosmologists combine supernovae, the CMB and baryon acoustic oscillations to constrain the expansion history. In your own words, explain how each depends on $H(z)$ and why combining them is more powerful than any one alone.
s3-l021-horizons-observations-lcdm.rubric: Full credit: (1) distances such as comoving/luminosity/angular-diameter distance are integrals of $1/H(z)$, so each probe constrains an integral of the expansion history; (2) supernovae give luminosity distance (standard candles) vs $z$, mainly sensitive to acceleration; CMB peaks and BAO provide standard rulers (angular scales) fixing curvature and matter density; (3) each probe has degeneracies in $\Omega_m$–$\Omega_\Lambda$–$H_0$ that are broken in combination (different directions in parameter space).
s3-l021-horizons-observations-lcdm.modelAnswer: Distances are integrals of $1/H(z)$, so each probe measures some combination of the density parameters in $H^2 = H_0^2[\Omega_m(1+z)^3 + \Omega_r(1+z)^4 + \Omega_k(1+z)^2 + \Omega_\Lambda]$. Supernovae (standard candles) measure luminosity distance versus redshift and are sensitive to acceleration; the CMB peaks and BAO are standard rulers, giving angular sizes that fix the geometry and matter density. Each leaves a degeneracy in the parameter space, but the degeneracy directions differ, so the intersection pins down $\Omega_m \approx 0.3$ and $\Omega_\Lambda \approx 0.7$.
